comment.value:
The authors present a database of wrist-located EMG recordings captured while participants performing typing tasks over multiple sessions (1,135 in total) on 108 subjects for benchmarking AR/VR typing activity. The dataset is provided through a link on AWS (297 GB as a zip archive) with partially commented Python code. 

The manuscript presents the dataset and also their findings through application of Machine learning models, and is of high quality.
The reviewers provided good feedback, which were addressed sufficiently by the authors, although I would like to see more information on  the design of experiment, and data collection in the author's updated paper (together with their other responses to the critiques).

They do differentiate their work from existing datasets, although holding a bar for a data set to have never existed seems overly restrictive to me, and will hold the field back or encourage people to throw out poorly documented and assembled databases just to say they are the first. (Something we see all too often in the tsunami of poorly assembled preprints we've seen over the last 10 years). If the dataset is sufficiently different (or even significantly adds to the volume in a field where the volume is low), and is accompanied by code and a good analysis of the data with benchmarking metrics, then this is contributing to the field. 

On the whole, I think the dataset is likely to enable forward motion in the field.

rebuttal.value:
> Typing on a physical keyboard already results in the intended action - a key press - and this action can be communicated accordingly to an external system. So it is not clear why EMG signals need to be detected to effectuate the key press on a physical keyboard.

> why the need to type without a keyboard and rely on EMG signals when the same can be achieved by simply typing on a physical keyboard and communicating the key press actions directly to the AR/VR environment.

Human computer interfaces for wearable/on-the-go computing paradigms such as AR/VR is a problem yet to be solved. New computing platforms consistently incorporate new modalities for input – e.g. mouse for early GUIs and touchscreens for smartphones. Future forms of on-the-go, wearable technologies such as AR/VR would render similar usability benefits from new, well-matched input modalities such as wrist EMG as pioneered in https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.02.23.581779v1.

Typing on a physical keyboard and communicating the key press actions to the AR/VR environment requires carrying a physical keyboard on oneself, defeating the transportability and convenience affordances of the AR paradigm. While transmitting key presses from a mobile keyboard can be an alternative solution, it comes at the cost of reduction in bandwidth compared to touch typing in traditional desktop settings. The other common solution of speech-to-text input is limited by social privacy implications. We discuss these in page 2 of the paper in Introduction.

> The dataset does not support the intended application the authors claim.

> If the intended application is “typing without a keyboard (wrists resting on laps or a flat surface)”, then the experiment design and dataset needs to be constructed accordingly to determine the real-world feasibility of such an application.

As mentioned in the Limitations section of the paper, we acknowledge that the dataset, having been collected on a physical keyboard, isn’t a precise replica of the target application domain: “[..] the dataset was collected using a physical keyboard on a desk, whereas real-world use cases would be aimed at removing physical constraints to enable seamless text entry such as typing while on the move or with hands on the lap [..]”.

But, one has to start somewhere, and we strongly argue that data collection while typing on a physical keyboard is a very reasonable place to start. The high-quality ground-truth afforded by this enables getting the system off the ground via off-the-shelf supervised learning techniques, which can subsequently be used to bootstrap adaptation to the precise target domain. For example, a highly performant supervised model trained with data collected while typing on a physical keyboard can then be used to generate pseudo-labels to enable training using data collected from typing on a flat surface without a physical keyboard. Repeatedly, ML application domains have followed such a strategy towards success – eg., the approach of pseudo-labeling is commonly used in ASR to train on speech data that lacks ground-truth but offers greater realism to a specific domain.

Moreover, our usage of Apple Magic Keyboard for data collection (as noted in Section 4) is very intentional in it has “short” keys that are closer to the surface than most other keyboards, making it a sufficiently close setup to typing on a flat surface. The reference provided in our earlier response - https://tech.facebook.com/reality-labs/2021/3/inside-facebook-reality-labs-wrist-based-interaction-for-the-next-computing-platform/ - includes a real demonstration of typing with sEMG on a flat surface without a physical keyboard, achieved in part with the help of data collected by typing on a physical keyboard.

> There are still ethical issues: “participants were compensated pursuant to their agreement with their employer”, “The vendor company hired the participants and compensated them based on the notice and hourly payment they agreed upon with the participants.” The issue is not compensating participants, but the employer-employee relationship that creates a conflict.

We would appreciate it if Reviewer hCYB can be more precise about why, or what about, the employer-employee relationship creates a conflict.

Participants’ employment situation is one of the factors IRB considers when approving a study. While we acknowledge the sensitivity of the employer-employee relationship between the participants involved in the study and the third-party vendor company employed by Meta to coordinate participant recruitment, we ensure that this is performed ethically by following practices consistent with standard scientific human subjects-based research procedures in the field.

Reviewer has read the author rebuttal. Authors provided more details about the experiment, updated figure and comparison, provided statistical results. 

However, main concerns are still present:

- The dataset does not support the intended application the authors claim. Typing on a physical keyboard already results in the intended action - a key press - and this action can be communicated accordingly to an external system. So it is not clear why EMG signals need to be detected to effectuate the key press on a physical keyboard. This work is unrelated to brain-computer interfaces given the difference in the intended direct source signal (brain vs. muscle) used for control. There are different movements and forces generated by different motor actions. If the intended application is “typing without a keyboard (wrists resting on laps or a flat surface)”, then the experiment design and dataset needs to be constructed accordingly to determine the real-world feasibility of such an application. Also, why the need to type without a keyboard and rely on EMG signals when the same can be achieved by simply typing on a physical keyboard and communicating the key press actions directly to the AR/VR environment.  

- There are still ethical issues: “participants were compensated pursuant to their agreement with their employer”, “The vendor company hired the participants and compensated them based on the notice and hourly payment they agreed upon with the participants.” The issue is not compensating participants, but the employer-employee relationship that creates a conflict. 

Other
- If computational resources are an issue, suggest increasing fold partition size to present results across a wider range of participants. 

Reviewer will keep the same rating.

rebuttal.value:
We thank reviewer hCYB for the detailed comments which will improve our manuscript and the impact of our work.

We note four lines of concerns:
1. Ethics relating to participant compensation
2. Application relevance
3. Statistical significance of baselines
4. Clarity on certain topics

We now carefully address each:

> [1] This statement is confusing as to why there is employer involvement in a study: “External participants were compensated pursuant to their agreement with their employer.”

The mention of the employer paying external participants relates to a vendor company that Meta engaged to recruit and hire study participants in the NYC metropolitan area. The vendor company is a global, well-respected company that met Meta’s stringent procurement and vetting standards. The vendor company hired the participants and compensated them based on the notice and hourly payment they agreed upon with the participants. This setup was disclosed to the overseeing IRB during submission and they deemed it to be ethically appropriate by approving the study. We will include this in the paper.

> [2] The utility of the dataset is not clear. [..] What specific application will use sEMG collected at the wrists while typing [..]?

The application is typing without a keyboard (wrists resting on laps or a flat surface) in virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) settings where high bandwidth text input without a physical keyboard is highly useful. In contrast to prior sEMG systems that focus on neuroprosthetics or clinical settings, our focus is on a practical high bandwidth input interface for AR/VR that can work across the population. The revised manuscript will clearly emphasize this utility. The following references demonstrate AR/VR applicability using the same sEMG hardware as the dataset:
- https://tech.facebook.com/reality-labs/2021/3/inside-facebook-reality-labs-wrist-based-interaction-for-the-next-computing-platform/
- https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kx_nVrEKwTE
- https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.02.23.581779v1

> [3] Only mean and standard deviation reported [..] Cross-validation and inclusion of confusion maps would enhance the paper.

Thank you for emphasizing this. The key empirical claims in Table 2 with repeated measures statistical significance quantifications are:
a. Personalized models are more accurate than generic models: mean CER 55.38% -> 15.38% (p < .005)
b. Personalized models are more accurate when finetuned from a generic model: mean CER 15.38% -> 11.28% (p < .005),
c. Language model improves performance overall:
  - Generic: mean CER 55.38% -> 51.78% (p < .005)
  - Personalized random-init: mean CER 15.38% -> 9.55% (p < .005)
  - Personalized finetuned: mean CER 11.28% -> 6.95% (p < .005)

As suggested, the paper could be improved through K-fold cross-validation beyond the n=8 test users. We note that the test user CER is not the fundamental contribution of the work, but rather a standardized baseline for the community to use for the given split. Our benchmark focuses on this 100 train/8 test user split to facilitate accessibility of experimentation - a single A/B comparison entailing training K=108/8 generic and N*K personalized models might be a considerable amount of computation for some research groups. Nevertheless, the generate_splits.py script included in the repo makes it easy to (re)generate splits with different sets of test users for cross-validation experiments.

> [4] Visual needed for the sEMG electrode systems and electrodes annotated [..]

An updated Fig 1 is provided in the attached pdf, and the paper will be amended as such.

> [4] specify the filtering parameters

The analog filtering parameters are mentioned in Section 4: “bandpass filtered with -3 dB cutoffs at 20 Hz and 850 Hz before digitization”. The digital highpass filter has 40Hz cutoff, which we will clarify in the text.

> [4] Define acronyms in figure/table captions.

Thank you, we will address this in the paper.

> [4] Authors discuss how their work differ from previous contributions, but comparison needs to be more comprehensive [..]. Suggest including a table [..]

A comparison table is now provided in the attached pdf, and will be included in the paper.

> [4] Relevance to brain-computer interface systems is not clear [..].

The relevance is surrounding the fact that BCIs have been imagined as a potential to interface more directly with computers bypassing intermediate devices such as keyboards. Task-wise, a close parallel to our work as noted in Section 3 is Willett et al. (2021) demonstrating an intracortical BCI for text generation for a single subject with a paralyzed hand. Our work focuses similarly on text generation, but outside of the clinical setting targeting consumer products. For a more detailed treatment of the connections with BCI, “Related work in HCI and BCI” section of https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.02.23.581779v1 serves as a reference.

> [4] Authors mention issues of "missing sEMG due to Bluetooth failures", which need to be elaborated on given the intended real-time application.

While data collection requires streaming sEMG via bluetooth for model training, the advent of edge compute for ML inference makes it possible to circumvent bluetooth during deployment. This setup has other advantages too: user privacy with sEMG not leaving the wrist device, avoiding latency of streaming given real-time application needs. We will clarify this under Future Directions.

> [4] sEMG signals are still susceptible to motion artifacts [..]. Artifact identification noted [..] but not addressed during actual implementation.

While the dataset recordings are tagged with detected artifacts as noted in Datasheet, for generalization to the real world domain where motion artifacts are unavoidable, our models are trained with the inclusion of these artifacts. Our results demonstrate that it is possible to recognize keystrokes in the presence of these artifacts.

rebuttal.value:
We would like to thank reviewer zAj9 for endorsing our work. We address each concern below:

> The manuscript is written with little information about the design of experiment [..]

We remark that “Data Collection Setup” in Section 4 is a faithful reproduction of our experimental design. Unlike prior datasets that have a more rigid experimental setup, the uniqueness of ours lies in a naturalistic task closely reflecting real-word behavior. Our experimental results show that, despite the relatively unconstrained experimental protocol, we are able to obtain usable models owing to dataset scale.

> The variability in number of sessions, duration per individual etc. make the utility of the dataset limited [..]

It is indeed true that there is variability in the duration of data per subject as noted in Table 1. Collecting more sessions for certain subjects allowed us to quantify the impact of the amount of data per participant on model performance. Yet, it is feasible to rerun analysis with a fixed duration of data per subject. A fixed 2 hours of data per subject would still lead to a dataset containing 94 subjects, 1.5 hours to a dataset containing 101 subjects, and 1 hour to a dataset containing 104 subjects. This can be inspected by running the print_dataset_stats.py included in the repo, and custom data splits can be regenerated via the generate_splits.py script.

We propose to add the following paragraph to the Limitations section:

“Dataset shared contains all data collected on 108 subjects participating in the study, with the amount of data per subject being variable as noted in Table 1. While this allows one to more easily study the performance of personalized models, it can create generic models that are better optimized for a subset of the population. From an ML perspective, however, we consistently observed that using as much training data as possible leads to better model performance. For experiments that demand keeping the amount of data per subject constant, we note that n=94 out of the 108 participants in the dataset have 2 hours of more data per subject”.

> The manuscript does mention the usage of the dataset by neuroscience community. However, they do not account for many facts both from natural language processing point of view [..]

It is true that language studies in neuroscience carefully curate text stimuli to control for certain confounding factors. Here, as stated in the manuscript, the stimuli consisted of “words sampled randomly from a dictionary as well as sentences sampled from English Wikipedia (after filtering out offensive terms)”. Note that our dataset consists of more than 5.2 million keystrokes, roughly a million words. Owing to the size, we expect a similar distribution of character and n-gram frequencies as English Wikipedia. This is orders of magnitude larger than most neuroimaging language studies except potentially the ones using natural stimuli such as Tang et al 2023 (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-023-01304-9) that used podcasts as audio stimuli. Such related works also do not control for word/letter frequencies yet consider analysis that involve such factors. See for example works like this one https://nbdt.scholasticahq.com/article/38668-deep-recurrent-encoder-an-end-to-end-network-to-model-magnetoencephalography-at-scale where permutation importance can be used to probe the impact of certain factors on model performance.

> The construction of the dataset is merely focussed on the volume of the data rather than systematic collection as compared to visiting similar datasets which are more well organized.

Prior datasets do tend to have greater task systematism such as a relatively small set of gestures repeated a certain number of times. In contrast, our work intentionally aims for greater ecological validity, with a focus on natural typing behavior rather than a rigid enforcement of typing out individual characters or n-grams for certain repetitions. We believe that this naturalistic setting contributes to the uniqueness and real-world relevance of our dataset.

Our focus on the dataset volume is motivated by our observation that, as with other ML domains such, scale is crucial for out-of-the-box generalization of sEMG models to unseen users (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.02.23.581779v1). The volume of our dataset being an order of magnitude larger than prior ones makes it possible to benchmark our models across subjects, whereas existing datasets tend to focus on evaluation within the same subject.

> The paper is written with clarity sufficient for a regular paper, but not enough clarity for a dataset paper. More documentation on the dataset should have been included in the paper.

We appreciate the author for encouraging us to improve the clarity of the dataset documentation in the paper. While we note that the README file in the code repo, the scripts provided, and the detailed code comments provide in-depth documentation, we acknowledge the paper can reflect this better and plan to include it in the Appendix.

> It is not really clear what is the contribution beyond being a larger dataset compared to prior work.

Thank you for requesting this clarification. We cover this in Section 3: “While there are several public sEMG datasets, emg2qwerty is unique in its hardware properties, scale, and the type of participant activity [..]”.

Beyond scale, our sEMG hardware is unique in its consumer-grade practicality while still providing signal quality and sampling rate matching clinical levels. Our focus on the rapidly time-varying task of typing rather than static gestures makes our dataset much more temporally dense in activity compared to prior work. Finally, our focus on the naturalistic task of typing adds to the real world relevance of our dataset compared to many existing ones that focus on abstract hand gestures. We believe these properties make our dataset novel, more broadly relevant, and appealing.

We would like to thank reviewer mbq7 for their enthusiastic review about our work, judging our work as “well written”, and “covering the relevant literature” while seeing the potential of our approach as a “desirable solution for human-computer communication”.

We now address concerns with inline comments:

> Was there any inclusion criteria for the user on typing accuracy considering the necessity of touch typing for robust predictions? Comments on how that could impact the benchmarks would be insightful.

We appreciate you calling this out to improve the clarity of our dataset and benchmarks! Data collection participants were initially screened for their touch typing ability via self-reporting, and only those with the ability to touch type without looking at the keyboard, and achieve the correct finger to key mapping at least about 90% of the time (as self-reported by looking at a color-coded QWERTY keyboard pictorial) were included in the study. Subjects passing the self-reported questionnaire subsequently took part in a typing test, and only those meeting adequate typing speed and accuracy levels were included in the study.

While we ensured that the participants were sufficiently proficient in touch typing, in the spirit of making the dataset realistic for broader usage where the majority of real world touch typists aren’t perfect in their finger to key mapping, we do not enforce a rigid constraint beyond the aforementioned self-reported 90% finger to key mapping correctness followed by a touch typing screening test to filter participants based on their speed and accuracy. We will clarify this in the paper upon acceptance.

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper describes, emg2qwerty, a dataset of surface electromyography (sEMG) signals collected from the left and right wrists during typing (US) English sentences on a QWERTY keyboard. File content includes (left and right) sEMG, ground truth key logger sequence and corresponding time stamps of the signals. Data from 108 individuals are included. Dataset use is demonstrated by training machine learning models (generic and individual) to predict keystroke from sEMG signals.

review.value:
**Quality**

-    Large dataset size (108 participants) with training/validation/test partition outlined for train and test users. 

-    Data are provided with minimal post-processing with signals spanning the entire duration of the typing recording, which is good for reusability. Data files are provided in HDF5 format. Authors note that a script will be provided to convert to Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) format (open file format). 

- Experiments are described with enough detail for reproducibility. Results presented include character error rates (CERs) before and after language model correction for a generic model and subject-specific models with either random initialization or fine-tuning of the generic model.

- Performance reporting. The within-subject changes in character error rate (CER) is the measure of interest. Only mean and standard deviation reported. No statistical analysis to assess significance of results. Analysis needs to consider the repeated measures for each subject across conditions. Cross-validation and inclusion of confusion maps would enhance the paper.

**Clarity**

-  Paper is well written. 

-  Visual needed for the sEMG electrode systems and electrodes annotated accordingly in Figure 1.

**Originality**

- sEMG signals are collected from the wrist while typing, although relevant application is not clear.

**Significance**

- The utility of the dataset is not clear. What problem is being addressed? This is not clear from the extended introduction, background and related prior work included in the paper. What specific application will use sEMG collected at the wrists while typing or a related application? A potential scenario is individuals with hand amputations, but the dataset considerations would be much different even if including individuals with hands.

limitations.value:
- Authors acknowledge limitations include dataset generated touch typing English phrases/sentences on a QWERTY keyboard, typing force variability across users/keyboard models, and the use of proprietary sEMG hardware. 

- Limitations identified by reviewer mentioned above. 

- sEMG signals are still susceptible to motion artifacts (internal and external sources). Artifact identification noted for data quality of control but not addressed during actual implementation.

-  Authors mention issues of "missing sEMG due to Bluetooth failures", which need to be elaborated on given the intended real-time application.

clarity.value:
- The paper is well written. Captions of figures and tables describe content.
- A visual of the electrodes around both wristbands and their annotations in Figure 1. Also specify the filtering parameters.
- Define acronyms in figure/table captions.

relation_to_prior_work.value:
Authors discuss how their work differ from previous contributions, but comparison needs to be more comprehensive as some aspects are not necessarily comparable. Prior datasets were focused on sEMG applications for motor neuroprosthetics (includes missing limb scenario). There is also the difference between EMG signals collected on arm/forearm vs. wrist and specific application will influence gesture vocabulary. Suggest including a table to better summarise the similarities and differences. Is data from all the referenced work publicly available? It should be noted that most of the datasets include only individuals with intact limbs.

Relevance to brain-computer interface systems is not clear given the different signal types.

documentation.value:
- A description of the data collection is included in the paper. Dataset checklist and datasheet are provided in the supplement. 

- A link to download the dataset and code (in supplement file) are provided for review. However, the large dataset size (287GB?) is not practical for review. A dataset tree and sample files would have been useful for review. 

- Authors note that the code and the dataset will be made publicly available in the camera ready version. 

- Hosting (dataset on company platform, code on GitHub), licensing (CC-BY-NC-SA 4.0, requires signing licensing agreement before download) and maintenance plans are mentioned.

title.value: emg2qwerty: A Large Dataset with Baselines for Touch Typing using Surface Electromyography

abstract.value: Surface electromyography (sEMG) non-invasively measures signals generated by muscle activity with sufficient sensitivity to detect individual spinal neurons and richness to identify dozens of gestures and their nuances. Wearable wrist-based sEMG sensors have the potential to offer low friction, subtle, information rich, always available human-computer inputs. To this end, we introduce emg2qwerty, a large-scale dataset of non-invasive electromyographic signals recorded at the wrists while touch typing on a QWERTY keyboard, together with ground-truth annotations and reproducible baselines. With 1,135 sessions spanning 108 users and 346 hours of recording, this is the largest such public dataset to date. These data demonstrate non-trivial, but well defined hierarchical relationships both in terms of the generative process, from neurons to muscles and muscle combinations, as well as in terms of domain shift across users and user sessions. Applying standard modeling techniques from the closely related field of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), we show strong baseline performance on predicting key-presses using sEMG signals alone. We believe the richness of this task and dataset will facilitate progress in several problems of interest to both the machine learning and neuroscientific communities. Dataset and code can be accessed at https://github.com/facebookresearch/emg2qwerty.

venue.value: NeurIPS 2024 Track Datasets and Benchmarks Poster

TLDR.value: First large-scale public dataset (100+ users, 1000+ sessions, 346 hours) with baselines for QWERTY keyboard typing using surface electromyography (sEMG) for building non-invasive neuromotor interfaces as in wrist-based wearables

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
